stories.headline: NBA reveals $11B arena initiative to boost efforts for Europe league
stories.summary: The long-planned NBA-backed league in Europe took another step toward becoming reality with the unveiling of a plan that targets nearly $11 billion in funding for the development and renovation of arenas around the continent.
stories.body:
The long-planned NBA-backed league in Europe took another step toward becoming reality Wednesday with the unveiling of a plan that targets at least 10 billion euros (nearly $11 billion) in funding for the development and renovation of arenas around the continent.

The NBA said a group of global investment firms -- including Apollo Sports Capital, Ares Management, Arctos, Blackstone, HPS Investment Partners, J.P. Morgan, Sixth Street and Stonepeak -- are supporting the initiative. It will, the league said, provide "prospective clubs and ownership groups with access to sustainable capital and the NBA's expertise to develop modern arena facilities and, where appropriate, surrounding districts."

The NBA and FIBA, which are partnering to launch the European league, have said it will begin play next fall.

"We've seen firsthand how state-of-the-art arenas and the related developments around them can transform basketball teams and their surrounding communities," NBA commissioner Adam Silver said. "As we prepare to launch a new league in Europe alongside FIBA, we see a significant opportunity to help clubs develop facilities which both build on the unique traditions that define European basketball while also elevating the fan experience and attracting many more live events."

The investors will partner with "participating clubs, ownership groups, local developers and other service providers to develop world-class arenas" that would become year-round destinations, the NBA said.

In a collective statement, the investors said they would help honor "the passion and traditions of European basketball fans and supporting lasting economic growth in the communities where the game means so much."

The NBA and FIBA have taken on the Europe project in large part because they believe the potential -- both from a commercial standpoint and a competitive one -- is not close to being realized. A new league has been talked about for years, with a plan to move forward getting announced in March 2025. Many of the NBA's top players of this era, including San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama (France), Miami's Giannis Antetokounmpo (Greece), the Lakers' Luka Doncic (Slovenia) and Denver's Nikola Jokic (Serbia), hail from Europe.

The NBA has long maintained that world-class arenas can drive immense growth -- thousands of jobs, millions of tickets, billions in economic impact -- not just for basketball franchises but also for the cities where they are located as centers of economic and cultural activities. Those arenas aren't easy to find in Europe, at least compared to more state-of-the-art venues in the U.S.

Current target countries for the NBA-FIBA endeavor are known to include Britain (potential host cities of London and Manchester), France (Paris and Lyon), Spain (Madrid and Barcelona), Italy (Rome and Milan), Germany (Munich and Berlin), Greece (Athens) and Turkey (Istanbul). None of those cities have been formally announced as NBA Europe selections.

stories.headline: NHL Thanksgiving Panic Index: Which teams should be most worried?
stories.summary: Teams in playoff position on the holiday tend to stay there (77.1% since 2013-14). Who is in the best and worst shape?
stories.body:
At Thanksgiving, you either have a seat at the table or you don't. The same thing applies to Stanley Cup playoff berths: If teams don't have a seat at the table when the calendar flips to Turkey Day, the odds aren't in their favor.

Since the NHL switched the wild-card format in 2013-14, roughly 77% of the teams in playoff seeds at American Thanksgiving eventually appeared in the postseason. In 2025-26, 12 of the 16 teams in playoff positions made the cut.

There's still hope for those teams outside the bubble. Since the NHL expanded to 30-plus franchises, multiple teams every season made the playoffs while outside the picture at Thanksgiving. Over the past 10 seasons, 22 teams have rallied to make the playoffs after sitting outside the playoff picture at U.S. Thanksgiving.

There have even been six teams since 1995 that overcame deficits of seven points or more at Thanksgiving to make the playoffs -- the last one being the Edmonton Oilers in 2023, who were 10 points out.

So there's some hope, but there's also cause for concern -- and in some cases outright panic. Heck, even the teams in playoff seeds have their own anxieties.

Here is the American Thanksgiving NHL Panic Index, measuring the alarm for all 32 teams and organizing them into tiers. Let's start with the one team having a serene and blissful Thanksgiving in the standings.

Complete nirvana
Carolina Hurricanes

Imagine being the reigning Stanley Cup champions and then dominating the NHL after 24 games the following season, with basically the same groups of players. That is the Zen of the Carolina Hurricanes.

Their .813 points percentage (18-3-3) was tops in the league entering Wednesday night's games, with an NHL best plus-45 in goal differential. They appear poised for a potential repeat -- and you know GM Eric Tulsky and his front office aren't afraid to aggressively augment a roster that's already Cup-worthy.

Zero panic
Edmonton Oilers

Minnesota Wild

Vegas Golden Knights

The Wild led the NHL in points (41) entering Wednesday's games, while trailing only the Hurricanes in points percentage (.788) and goal differential (plus-37). Minnesota is 12-0-3 in their last 15 games (.900 points percentage!).

They have one of the league's most dominant offensive players in Kirill Kaprizov, whose 15-game point streak set a new franchise standard; one of the best goaltenders in Jesper Wallstedt, with a .924 save percentage and a 16-2-4 record; and one of the best defensemen in Quinn Hughes, who had 34 points in 24 games before the injury bug bit him. No, they don't have Dylan Larkin. But they have the assets they would have traded for Dylan Larkin, which means GM Bill Guerin will still go center shopping to complete his Cup-contending lineup.

After 26 regular-season games, Connor McDavid was projected to finish with 187 points. Adjusted for era, I'd say that's a gentlemen's 200 points. Regardless, Edmonton led the Pacific heading into American Thanksgiving, with over a dozen-point cushion over the fourth-place team. What's scary is that the Oilers are also a top-10 team defensively, thanks in part to Tristan Jarry and Devon Levi, who sorta-kinda-maybe could be the goalies that finally give Edmonton the stability they need in the crease.

Vegas nearly slipped to the next tier. The Golden Knights have their flaws -- less-than-elite team stats, a lack of scoring from their blue line, analytically fraught goaltending -- but they also have one incredible virtue: Playing in the Pacific Division. They were second to the Oilers and a country mile ahead of everyone else entering the American Thanksgiving cutoff.

Well, make that two virtues: Vegas has been uncharacteristically healthy for the most part this season. Even if that changes, please see virtue No. 1 for why that won't sink them. Stathletes projects Vegas with a 99.9% chance of making the playoffs.

Panicked but relatively pleased
Boston Bruins

Dallas Stars

Montreal Canadiens

New Jersey Devils

St. Louis Blues

Tampa Bay Lightning

All of these teams were in or right around playoff spots as the turkeys hit the tables in the U.S. In most cases, this was entirely predictable even before the season.

There's been more attention paid to disgruntled Lightning winger Nikita Kucherov's body language on the bench than to the fact that his team were a few percentage points from the Atlantic Division lead. Kucherov, Jake Guentzel and Brandon Hagel offensively and Andrei Vasilevskiy between the pipes are all key reasons why.

Just a shade behind the Lightning were the Canadiens, an Eastern Conference finalist last season. Before this week, the greatest development for the Habs was the arrival of Jacob Fowler as an NHL goaltending force and a rookie of the year favorite. But this week has all been about the arrival of Dylan Larkin, giving Montreal the elite center depth -- along with Nick Suzuki and Phillip Danault -- to contend with the league's elite teams in the postseason.

The Devils and Stars are a bit further back from their respective division leaders, but have to both be feeling pretty good about the first quarter of their seasons. New Jersey is buying newly acquired Connor Hellebuyck some time to find his game -- after missing the preseason and first month of the season -- with the fourth-best offense in the NHL, led by 30 points in 24 games for Jack Hughes.

The Stars are a mirror image of the Devils: They've had the goaltending all season in Jake Oettinger (plus-12.3 goals saved above expected, per Money Puck) but had the 25th-best offense through 23 games. The bottom line in both cases: These teams are finding ways to win.

The Bruins and Blues weren't playoff favorites in preseason prognostications, but here we are. Boston was in a playoff seed at Thanksgiving. The Blues are right on the bubble, having won four straight games.

The fascinating thing about Boston is its offensive balance. We all knew David Pastrnak was going to lead the team in points by a significant margin. But the Bruins had nine players through 23 games in double-digit points and saw Elias Lindholm -- a player who tapped out at 17 goals in each of the last two seasons -- match Pastrnak with 11 goals.

Meanwhile in St. Louis, Robert Thomas remains one of the NHL's most underappreciated offensive wagons, playing to a point-per-game pace while turning linemate Jimmy Snuggerud into a star, assisting on eight of his 14 goals.

Panicked until they're healthy again
Colorado Avalanche

Florida Panthers

New York Rangers

The Panthers are merely visiting this tier as they get two of their best players back from injury. Consider them "panicked but relatively pleased" after Wednesday.

Aleksander Barkov and Brad Marchand have both been cleared by team doctors to return to Florida's lineup. Both players have been limited to just two games this season. In Marchand's absence, his center Anton Lundell has found a spot between the Tkachuk brothers. Marchand is expected to skate with center Sam Bennett. We report this to give the rest of the league fair warning.

Cale Makar's return to the Avalanche couldn't have come at a more opportune time, as star center Nathan MacKinnon's injury recovery timeline was extended to 12 weeks. Colorado had a .630 points percentage through 23 games, which is a decent early-season cushion. Now their depth will be tested with Nate Dogg on the shelf for months.

The Rangers are here not because their current lineup faces any injury calamities. But all the success the Blueshirts have had -- which put them right around a playoff seed by Thanksgiving -- is undercut by the season-ending injury to star goalie Igor Shesterkin. Without him, there's a ceiling as to how good the Rangers are and could be this season. Wait 'til next year.

Panicked because their goaltending stinks
Anaheim Ducks

Utah Mammoth

Washington Capitals

Through 25 games, the Ducks had the league's worst team save percentage (.853). Last season, Lukas Dostal was their safety net. This season, he's playing like someone cut a hole in that net (minus-5.55 goals saved above expected via Stathletes). Ville Husso hasn't been much better. Anaheim simply doesn't have the team defensive prowess to sustain that kind of goaltending performance.

The Mammoth are giving up more goals (3.32 per game) than they're scoring (3.28) on average because of absolutely putrid goaltending. They rode Karel Vejmelka into the playoffs last season. His game has fallen apart this season, with an .872 save percentage and minus-5.8 goals saved above expected. Fans have clamored for Sebastian Cossa to rescue them. His analytics are generally just as bad; according to Stathletes, they're even worse (minus-7.8 goals saved above expected) than Vejmelka.

The Capitals could have qualified for several of these tiers in what's been a disastrous recent run of play and an overall bummer of a season. They can't find offensive cohesion, their blue line has been porous and Alex Ovechkin has scored as many goals as Igor Shesterkin this season during a not-all-that-fond farewell tour.

But in a rather stunning development, one of the league's best goalie tandems has been mediocre. Logan Thompson (.878 save percentage) and Charlie Lindgren (.849) are both in the negative analytically and have combined to give the Capitals the season-worst team save percentage in the league through 21 games.

Regression panicked
Nashville Predators

New York Islanders

Ottawa Senators

Seattle Kraken

Winnipeg Jets

PDO is a hockey metric that combines a team's shooting percentage and save percentage into a single number. It's considered a measure of "puck luck," while also acting as a predictor of sorts: Teams with an uncharacteristically high PDO are bound to regress to the mean, while those below average should swing upward at some point.

The Senators had the fifth-highest PDO in the NHL through 25 games, fueled by the third best 5-on-5 team save percentage thanks to Linus Ullmark. Their shooting percentage is above last season's levels as well.

The Kraken (sixth) and Islanders (seventh) are also riding the PDO train, with both shooting above their percentages from last season. The Kraken are in a more tenuous position, as they're underwater in several analytic categories (percentage of shot attempts, expected goals percentage among them).

The Jets were third in PDO over their last 10 games, going 8-1-1 in that span while shooting a preposterous 15.1% at 5-on-5. That'll obviously come back down to terra firma at some point.

The Predators are eighth in PDO over their last 10 games, but they face a more pressing question of sustainability: Can a team this top-heavy offensively compete for a playoff spot? Filip Forsberg, Steven Stamkos, Roman Josi and Ryan O'Reilly all have over 20 points; no other Predators skater had more than 10 heading into Wednesday.

Nihilistically panicked
Calgary Flames

Detroit Red Wings

Pittsburgh Penguins

Vancouver Canucks

All four of these teams are already tabulating their draft lottery odds, and that's probably fine.

The Flames and Canucks are in a rebuild. The Red Wings might as well be in one as they bid adieu to Dylan Larkin and bonjour to Michael Hage after their trade with Montreal.

The Penguins were a playoff teams last season and would have liked to be one again, but GM Kyle Dubas was a realist in his news conference last week, saying Pittsburgh would be focused on "future-oriented" moves. "We have to continue to make sure that this team isn't a decade-long in the abyss," he said. Sometimes, you lose to win.

Extremely panicked
Buffalo Sabres

Los Angeles Kings

Philadelphia Flyers

San Jose Sharks

The Kings brought on head coach Peter Laviolette to try to extend their playoff qualification streak to six seasons, but he can't even tease out a playoff push from this roster. Through 22 games, the Kings were third to last in the conference.

One of the reasons both MoneyPuck (43.8%) and Stathletes (70.3%) give Los Angeles decent playoff odds is because someone has to finish third in the Pacific Division. Stathletes gives the Sharks a 20.9% chance of making the postseason, but San Jose has yet to locate its swagger and stride after being a preseason glamour pick. We knew they'd struggle defensively. That they're 28th in goals per game is the real stunner.

But the Sharks are outscoring the Flyers so far this season. Last spring, Philly made the playoffs and won a round. Five months later, fans are flying airplanes with banners calling for coach Rick Tocchet to be fired, while team executives are flying across Canada to make sure Matvei Michkov doesn't want to be traded.

The Sabres broke the longest playoff drought in NHL history last season, lost a couple of key players and are now trying to claw their way back into the wild-card race. Stathletes gives them a 20.6% chance of making the playoffs, which means there's around an 80% chance all the good vibes from last season get swallowed up like a small car in a Western New York blizzard.

Beyond panicked
Chicago Blackhawks

Columbus Blue Jackets

Toronto Maple Leafs

The Blackhawks were supposed to crawl out of the primordial ooze of their rebuild this season. Injuries to Connor Bedard and Bowen Byram, combined with not being a good hockey team at all, scuttled those hopes.

The Blue Jackets nearly made the playoffs last season, but the vibes have been horrible every moment after that. Norris winner Zach Werenski expressed doubt about his future with the team. Winger Kirill Marchenko was traded upon request. Stathletes gives Columbus a 1.2% chance of making the playoffs. That's bad!

Yet not as bad as the team to whom they traded Marchenko, the Maple Leafs, who had a 0.2% chance of making the playoffs heading into Wednesday night. The Leafs could have been in the "panicked because their goaltending stinks" tier, seeing as how Sergei Bobrovsky's atrocious season (minus-6.98 goals saved above expected) has cost Toronto dearly. But the Leafs have problems that extend well beyond the crease. Coach Jim Hiller was hired by new GM John Chayka. He might not make it through this season.

Now that's a panic move.

In summary: Love it for Montreal, quantity over quality for Detroit, and some real questions about that whole panic over no-trade clauses when the Red Wings held the line and Larkin eventually blinked.

PUCK HEADLINES
DATELINE: Michigan
I didn't appreciate the people who wanted to pour salt in the Red Wings' wound over the Larkin trade by suggesting University of Michigan center Michael Hage -- the centerpiece of that trade return from Montreal -- might opt never to sign a contract with his new rightsholder. Furthermore, there were people entertaining the idea that Hage would become an NCAA free agent ... and eventually sign with Montreal. That's just cruel.

It was also nonsensical. Detroit interim GM Shawn Horcoff had to have some understanding with Hage prior to making the trade with Montreal, or else he's not making that trade. Like, perhaps, from his son Will Horcoff, who is Hage's housemate and teammate at Michigan?

Hage himself ended the drama in an interview with Nick Cotsonika of NHL.com, saying he plans to sign with the Red Wings after Michigan's season is over. "After, hopefully, we win a national championship," he said.

And hopefully that puts the speculation to bed.

DATELINE: PITTSBURGH
When Penguins GM Kyle Dubas spoke with the media last week, the topic of Sidney Crosby's future naturally came up. The captain is 39. He's scored 15 points in 23 games for a Penguins team near the bottom of the Eastern Conference. He's averaging under 20 minutes per game for the second straight season.

Most crucially, he's an unrestricted free agent next summer, on a team that's going to trade away a handful of veterans for "future-oriented" assets.

"I think in Sid's case, he's as unique as it gets," Dubas said. "We want to get into this as far as we can, have an indication about where we're at and where we're going, and make sure everyone's comfortable with that. He's owed all the respect in the world. If he wants to be here, that's great, and that's obviously what we would love as well."

But Dubas also stressed that Crosby, Evgeni Malkin and Kris Letang are "at an age where it's not just a given they're going to keep playing. We all wish them to play forever but, at some point, the time comes."

Crosby's agent Pat Brisson told Sportsnet's "Real Kyper and Bourne" show on Monday that Sid's goal is only play for the Penguins.

"Kyle came out last week and said he's going to trade for futures. He has a responsibility right now to move these parts that he's going to move," Brisson said. "Sid is evaluating and watching. His goal is to be a Penguin forever. That's always been his goal. That's why he's in no rush."

When people talk about Crosby leaving a losing team to play for a Cup contender, the thing they miss is that the losing team is the Pittsburgh Penguins. The team that drafted Crosby, where he won three Stanley Cups, where he's comfortable and where he's never wavered in wanting to play his entire career.

Again, he's 39. The writing has been on the wall in Pittsburgh for quite some time, having not won a playoff series since 2018. I've long believed -- maybe hoped -- Crosby would end up on a contender for one last championship push before his Mount Puckmore-worthy career ends.

But I'm starting to believe that, like Brisson said, Crosby will be a Penguin forever. I've come around to the idea he wants to end his run with the same organization with whom he began it. Maybe he's won enough where mentorship will be as rewarding as another playoff run. Maybe he wants to act as the bridge between eras in Pittsburgh.

Or, and please understand I hope this isn't the case: Maybe we're watching the farewell tour now and don't even realize it. As Dubas said: "At some point, the time comes."

stories.headline: Pep Guardiola: Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo rivalry prolonged their careers
stories.summary: Pep Guardiola believes Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi would not have enjoyed such long and dominant careers without each other.
stories.body:
Pep Guardiola said he believes Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi would not have enjoyed such long and dominant careers without each other.

Ronaldo and Messi's rivalry dominated football for over a decade as they racked up a combined 13 Ballon d'Or awards and established themselves as the best two players of their generation.

They battled while representing Real Madrid and Barcelona (when Guardiola managed the Catalan club) respectively and featured at last summer's World Cup despite being in the twilight of their careers, before both retiring from international football.

"I think the two of them helped each other a great deal, if Messi hadn't had Cristiano, or if Cristiano hadn't had Messi, their careers would likely have been shorter," Guardiola told former Brazil forward Romario.

"But they had each other in their rearview mirrors, watching what the other was doing made them think: 'I want to be better than him, I want to win more than him.'"

Ronaldo, 41, retired from Portugal duty as the leading men's international goal scorer and appearance-maker after 146 goals in 234 games.

The 'Ballon d'Or of All-Time' winner, Ronaldo celebrated his 987th career goal when he scored for Al Nassr in Tuesday's AFC Champions League.

"Another competitive animal, someone who cares about nothing else than winning and proving himself," Guardiola said of Ronaldo.

"A goalscorer. With his right foot, his left foot, his head, he's extraordinary."

Guardiola never worked with Ronaldo but did coach Messi for four seasons at Barcelona.

He credits the Argentinian forward for much of his success while in charge of the Catalan giants.

- Cristiano Ronaldo goal tracker: Road to 1,000 career goals

- Columbus coach says Messi should've got red card in Miami loss: 'Everyone knows'

In a remarkable spell, Guardiola led Barça to 14 trophies, including two Champions Leagues and three La Liga titles.

Asked what enabled him to rack up so many titles as a coach, Guardiola said: "Messi! When you have such good players, you become good yourself. As a coach, you have to ensure that everyone follows the same path, understanding how they get along and which players can be paired together to make things work. But I've been with three incredible teams, all with incredible players, that's why we won."

After leaving Barça, Guardiola steered Bayern Munich to Bundesliga crowns in each of his three seasons at the club, including two domestic doubles, before enjoying a trophy-laden decade in charge of Manchester City, the club he left in the summer.

Asked if he tried to sign Messi after he departed Barcelona in 2012, Guardiola said: "No, I never reached out to him. I'm a Barça fan."

Guardiola said he is in awe of Messi, a record eight-time Ballon d'Or winner, who led Argentina to 2022 World Cup glory then, aged 39, helped the defending champions to the final last summer when they lost to Spain.

"I have never seen a player like him, someone with the ability to score three goals and provide three assists every three days," he said. "Very few are capable of such consistency, and he would do it in training, too, during small-sided games. In four years of coaching, I never saw him miss a single training session. He possessed this incredible competitive drive, that is what set him apart."

Guardiola likened Messi, now the captain of MLS side Inter Miami, to basketball legend Michael Jordan.

"When we all watched the Michael Jordan documentary, it struck me that a young Jordan was very much like Messi: someone who, alongside his teammates, was driven to be the absolute best," he said.

For Guardiola, there is no player that could ever reach Messi's level. He said: "No one, there are many good ones but I don't see anyone reaching that level; performing at such a high standard every three days for 15 to 20 years, and I don't think I ever will.

"There are records that people said would never be broken, yet they eventually are. [Former Jamaican sprinter] Usain Bolt's records will be broken one day, too, but to maintain that level of play for so many years, with that kind of plasticity... I just don't see it."

stories.headline: Is your team out of the MLS playoffs? Adopt these chaos clubs as your 2nd side
stories.summary: Your favorite team isn't going to win MLS Cup, so we dug into our catalog of statistics to pinpoint three chaos clubs to follow for the postseason.
stories.body:
Let's be honest: Your favorite team isn't going to win MLS Cup this season.

Out of 30 clubs, 16 qualified for the ongoing Round 1 series, and of those playoff invitees, only one will lift the trophy next month. The odds aren't in your favor, so what's a fan to do when considering other teams to follow? And more importantly: What if you just want to be entertained when looking at the rest of the bracket?

We've got you covered. Here at ESPN, we've leaned into MLS After Dark vibes and dug into our detailed catalog of season-wide statistics to pinpoint three chaos clubs to follow during the playoffs. This isn't a list of title favorites, instead it's teams that willingly -- or in some cases, unwillingly -- showcase last-minute plot twists, controversy and disorganized performances.

It can all be messy and uncontrolled, but that's part of the beauty of an unpredictable league like MLS.

Ready to embrace some chaos? Let's dive in.

Late drama and stoppage-time fireworks: FC Cincinnati

Game-winning and game-tying goals: Ranked 1st

Stoppage-time goals: Ranked 1st

Goals scored minutes 76-90: Ranked 1st

Goals scored against minutes 76-90: Ranked 6th (tied)

Comeback wins: Ranked 4th (tied)

Points dropped from winning positions: Ranked 3rd

Stoppage-time madness, conceding and allowing late goals, dropping plenty of points but also capable of comebacks -- what more could you want?

Unsurprisingly, this constant push and pull for head coach Pat Noonan and his roster has led to Cincinnati narrowly sneaking into the playoffs after finishing ninth in the Eastern Conference. In the Wild Card play-in against Orlando City SC last week, we saw Cincinnati's season distilled into one match after conceding an early goal and then scoring three goals themselves, including one in the 85th minute to secure the 3-1 victory.

Regardless of what happens as the obvious underdogs against the Supporters' Shield-winning Nashville SC in the remainder of the series that FCC leads 1-0, attacking names such as Evander and Kévin Denkey will make things interesting with their exploits in the final third.

Evander himself was recently blunt about how inconsistent things have looked in 2026, but also confident that they could still make noise in the playoffs.

"There's been a lot of pressure on us throughout the whole season because, to be honest, we haven't had a good season," the Brazilian said after defeating Orlando. "And this is the time to change. I just told the boys to come out and enjoy the night. I think we need to enjoy the next upcoming games and try to save the season ... if we play like we played tonight, we can make it to the final."

Masters of the dark arts: Philadelphia Union
Fouls committed: Ranked 1st

Direct red cards: Ranked 4th (tied)

Yellow cards: Ranked 8th (tied)

Penalties won: Ranked 2nd (tied)

Penalties conceded: Ranked 13th (tied)

VAR events: Ranked 3rd (tied)

Looking for a bit of grit, penalties in favor, and shirt-pulling when the referee isn't looking? The Union are a perfect club for the dark arts when it comes to fans who are eager to watch a scrappy side that pushes the envelope.

And by scrappy, this isn't necessarily what someone might call a "dirty" style of play. It's high pressing, it's galvanized by a youthful core that includes the likes of up-and-coming U.S. men's national team players such as Cavan Sullivan and Neil Pierre, and it's been effective with a strong finish to the second half of the regular season.

What's interesting to note is that despite leading the league in fouls committed, they're eighth in yellow cards, pointing to the squad being more clever with their stoppages in play, as opposed to just recklessly diving into challenges and duels. In the face of that lengthy list of fouls, they're also only ranked at 13th when it comes to conceding penalties against them.

For comparison, Philadelphia has given up five penalties against this season, which is fewer than four other playoff teams and half of the league-leading total.

Those VAR situations are still ever-present, though, creating some edge-of-your seat moments in 2026.

At the very least, the Union are worth watching when it comes to Sullivan, their teenage star. Bound for Manchester City once he turns 18, the attacking midfielder has been effective with 14 goal contributions in his past 14 appearances.

No clean sheet goalfest: Inter Miami CF

Goals scored: Ranked 1st

Total goals scored and against: Ranked 3rd

Total xG for and against: Ranked 3rd

xG: Ranked 3rd

Shots on goal: Ranked 2nd

Even with Lionel Messi, things can still be messy for Miami.

In order to find the last time the club earned a scoreless draw in all competitions, you would have to go back to March 14, when they drew (without their Argentine star) away from home against Charlotte FC. There was only one other 0-0 tie all season: three days before that in Nashville.

Clearly, if you're only looking for goals, Miami is the answer and Messi is the catalyst for the club's attacking efforts. The World Cup winner finished the regular season with an astounding tally of 26 goals and 16 assists across 32 appearances, meaning that if you're tuning in, you'll likely see him finding the back of the net or being involved in the chance creation of a game-changing moment.

And yet there's a reason why they finished third in the Supporters' Shield table.

Their defense has been highly questionable with the amount of goals that they've allowed. In fact, no team within the top 13 of that Supporters' Shield table has allowed more goals (59) than Miami.

Messi and friends will create plenty of opportunities in the final third, but can they shut out their opponents? That's an entirely different conversation and a reason to follow along with this now-deemed chaos club.

stories.headline: Superlatives for this MLB free agent class, from Lowe to Gausman
stories.summary: Next best move for Mets? Best free agency timing? We have a yearbook's worth of awards for the top MLB free agents.
stories.body:
We still have a week left of potential chaos before the expected lockout freezes all moves, so while we still have time, let's dig in to the MLB offseason with our annual free agent superlatives.

Not included: Tarik Skubal, the most superlative in this class. He's headed to the New York Mets, who will pay him, Juan Soto and Bo Bichette about the same as what the Milwaukee Brewers paid for their entire World Series-winning roster in 2026.

Best bet on a 32-year-old outfielder: Seiya Suzuki

In a weak year for position players, the top two are similar-looking outfielders: Suzuki and Randy Arozarena. Both will be entering their age-32 seasons, are coming off their best seasons (5.1 WAR for Suzuki, 5.7 for Arozarena), hit right-handed, received qualifying offers and are projected to receive four-year, $90 million contracts.

Among the teams possibly looking for a corner outfielder: the Philadelphia Phillies (25th in OPS from their corner outfielders), Baltimore Orioles (26th), Toronto Blue Jays (27th), Houston Astros (30th) and San Diego Padres (17th, but they would move Fernando Tatis Jr. to second base). The Seattle Mariners might look to replace Arozarena with Suzuki. Which one would you rather have?

First off, given their age, both are risky bets -- or, at the minimum, unlikely to repeat those 5-WAR seasons. Check out the number of position players 32 or older who had 4-or-more WAR in recent seasons (with outfielders or DHs in parenthesis):

2026: 5 (Mike Trout)

2025: 9 (Aaron Judge, George Springer, Kyle Schwarber)

2024: 4 (Judge, Marcell Ozuna)

2023: 2

2022: 5 (Springer)

As you can see, not many players are remaining at an All-Star level in their 30s -- and this list includes only two players who played 100 games in the outfield (Judge and Trout). Still, with so many teams desperate for outfield help, both will get paid.

Why Suzuki over Arozarena? Suzuki has a couple of advantages. First, plate discipline. Suzuki ranked in the 89th percentile in chase rate and 91st percentile in walk rate; Arozarena comes in at the 42nd percentile in chase rate and 63rd percentile in walk rate (although he was hit by 26 pitches to boost his OBP). Suzuki also has better bat speed. The second big one is defense. Suzuki had excellent metrics in 2026, and Arozarena has been consistently below average in recent seasons. Suzuki has also been consistent: He's one of six players with 20-plus home runs and an .800 OPS in each of the past four seasons. Arozarena is the better baserunner (even though Suzuki is faster) and has been extremely durable (averaging 154 games played the past five seasons), but Suzuki's bat is more likely to play over the next four years.

Best second baseman if the price is right: Jazz Chisholm Jr.

Nineteen teams finished with an OPS below .700 from their second basemen -- eight of them below .675 -- so there are teams that need help at the position. Chisholm, Brandon Lowe and Luis Arraez are on the market (and Ketel Marte is available via trade). Lowe, coming off back-to-back 30-homer seasons and improved defense, is the top guy, but here are ESPN's projected contracts:

Lowe (5.3 WAR, 32 years old): Four years, $80 million

Arraez (2.9 WAR, 30 years old): Three years, $54 million

Chisholm (1.7 WAR, 29 years old): Two years, $46 million

If Lowe repeats his 2026 numbers and the defense is for real, he'll make the biggest impact the next couple of seasons. But we're back to age here, too. Paying Lowe from his age-32 to age-35 seasons for what he did at 30 and 31 is the risk. Only six second basemen have hit 30 home runs in a season at 32 or older. The last to do it was Robinson Cano in 2016; Jay Bell, Bret Boone (twice) and Jeff Kent (twice) did it between 1999 and 2003 when everyone was hitting home runs; and then you have to go all the way back to Joe Gordon in 1948 and Rogers Hornsby in 1929.

Arraez is a three-time batting champ who hit .310 in 2026 and almost never strikes out, so he presents a nice change of pace with his contact ability, but his OBP isn't great and he doesn't provide much power. Statcast metrics suddenly loved his defense at second base, which will help him receive a better contract than the one-year, $12 million deal he had with the San Francisco Giants for 2026.

But he lacks Chisholm's power/speed/defense upside -- although, admittedly, Chisholm rarely does all three of those things at his best in the same season. He's the youngest and most athletic of the trio, and he had 4.1 WAR in 2025 and 2.9 in 2024, when he hit .250/.328/.456 while averaging 28 home runs and 36 stolen bases. He also has positional flexibility, able to slide to third base or center field. On a short-term deal, Chisholm could be a big addition.

Best fit for Chicago White Sox: Clay Holmes

The White Sox must have had some plan in place when they dumped Luis Castillo's contract on the Colorado Rockies. They included Davis Martin to make the trade work, so the idea had to be that they could sign a pitcher better than Martin. But, in a matter of a few hours Tuesday, Trevor Rogers and then Freddy Peralta and then Kaima Taira agreed to deals, leaving Michael King as the only remaining starter in the top 10 from our free agent ranking -- and he's widely expected to return to San Diego. How about trying to steal Holmes away from the Cubs? He has a 3.44 ERA in his two years as a starter and is a groundball machine who keeps home runs in check (he missed time this past season, but that was due to fractured right fibula after getting hit by a comebacker).

Player needed to get the Phillies over the top: Brandon Lowe

Ahh, we just pumped up Chisholm, but the Phillies are worried only about the immediate future -- so, for them, betting on Lowe and his power is the way to go. In this piece last year, we had Alex Bregman to the Phillies; he went on to sign with the Chicago Cubs. The Phillies should have listened to us. Yes, signing Lowe would create a bit of an infield logjam, but Bryson Stott can shift to third (as he did after the Phillies traded for Arraez). It does leave the lineup lefty heavy, but imagine the home run damage Lowe might do at Citizens Bank Park -- and Lowe is less risky (and a better defender) than Teruaki Sato, the slugger from Japan who had been linked to the Phillies before he landed with ... the Cubs.

The reliever everyone wants: Adrian Morejon

Morejon has been outstanding the past three seasons with the Padres, with a 2.58 ERA in 233⅓ innings and while flashing a dominant four-pitch profile with durability. Over those three seasons, he's third in FanGraphs WAR among relievers while leading all relievers in innings. Everyone saw what the Brewers did in the postseason with a trio of left-handed relievers, so their title run probably helped Morejon's free agency.

ESPN forecasted a four-year, $88 million contract, which would be a huge average salary for a reliever who has never been a closer. It would be the third-highest total value for a reliever, behind Edwin Diaz's $102 million deal with the Mets (which he later opted out of to sign with the Dodgers) and Josh Hader's $95 million deal with the Astros.

Now for the "but ..." part of this. Relievers are volatile, even good ones. Check out how the highest-paid relievers in 2026 fared:

Hader ($19M): 1.01 ERA, 26 saves

Diaz ($17M): 8.68 ERA, seven saves

Devin Williams ($16M): 4.43 ERA, 16 saves

Tanner Scott ($16M): 2.69 ERA, 25 saves

Raisel Iglesias ($16M): 2.55 ERA, 34 saves

Ryan Helsley ($14M): 4.11 ERA, 8 saves

Scott and Iglesias were the only two to stay healthy, and only three of the six were effective. The next group making between $12 million and $14 million included Robert Suarez (effective but injured), Pete Fairbanks (6.31 ERA), Blake Treinen (29 innings) and Jeff Hoffman (lost closer role, traded). Only Aroldis Chapman was effective and healthy from this group. That's 11 relievers making at least $12 million, and only four who earned their salary. Still want Morejon at $20-plus million per season?

The next best move for the Mets: Kevin Gausman

A quick glance at Gausman's 4.51 ERA might suggest he's in decline as he enters his age-36 season, but the peripheral numbers remain above average (184 strikeouts against 47 walks) and the stuff hasn't deteriorated much -- his fastball still averaged 93.8 mph and his splitter and slider still generated swing-and-miss rates above 36%. Most importantly, check out his innings since 2021: 192, 174, 181, 193, 177. That's 31-plus starts every season, the rare pitcher who posts all six months, every year. He did serve up 26 home runs this past year, so he's a better fit for a more pitcher-friendly park -- a return to Toronto, San Diego ... or Citi Field, where Gausman would slide in nicely behind Skubal and Nolan McLean.

Player most likely to help the Brewers repeat: Casey Mize

Milwaukee isn't going to change the way it operates -- it let Jake Bauers leave for the Boston Red Sox on an affordable four-year, $58 million contract. The Brewers simply aren't going to commit long-term money to a player in his 30s, no matter what he meant to their success (even Christian Yelich's deal expires after 2028, which will create even more payroll flexibility).

The Brewers might want a starting pitcher, though. They have depth they can dip into, but the only starters worth more than 1.3 WAR this past season were Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, so the Brewers are going to be careful with those young arms after the postseason run. Kyle Harrison was terrible in the second half, and Shane Drohan had significant injury issues in the minors in 2024 and 2025. Quinn Priester missed all of 2026.

Of course, the Brewers aren't going to spend big money on a free agent, which is why Mize could be the perfect fit. He's not exactly a reclamation project because he had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Detroit Tigers, but he fell apart after he was traded to the Padres (7.46 ERA in 10 starts). If any team can figure out what went wrong, it will be the Brewers -- and they could probably sign him on a relatively low-cost one-year deal. Mize is an extreme flyball pitcher, so their superb outfield defense will be a big help, and they could more comfortably go with a six-man rotation, especially early in the season.

Best free agent timing award: Ty France

An All-Star with the Mariners in 2022, France hit .247 over the next three seasons, producing just 1.3 WAR. At 31 years old, his career was in jeopardy, and he had to settle for a minor league contract with the Padres in 2026 just as spring training was kicking off. He made the team, worked his way into the starting lineup and was the Padres' best hitter, finishing with a .295/.363/.502 slash line and ranking 11th in the majors in wRC+ among hitters with 500 plate appearances.

Will teams buy in to the swing changes France made or view 2026 as a fluke season? The lack of offense available will help drive interest in him, plus he's a good defender at first base, so he should end up with a multiyear deal -- and the biggest payday of his career.

Player who will inevitably end up in Seattle: Alec Bohm

Every year, president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto signs a veteran free agent hitter. It never works out, but one of these years, the Mariners will have to luck into the right move to fortify their offensive depth. Dipoto already acquired Maikel Garcia to play third base, so all Bohm has to do is DH, preferably just against left-handed pitchers, because that's what he's good at, hitting .302/.351/.503 in his career against southpaws.

stories.headline: Raheem Sterling avoids jail for dangerous driving
stories.summary: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has avoided jail after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling from a balloon on a motorway during rush hour before crashing into a metal gate.
stories.body:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has avoided jail after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling from a balloon on a motorway during rush hour before crashing into a metal gate.

The 31-year-old gave no reaction as he was sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court for dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide on May 28.

He was also ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

A driver who called police said he was "shocked" by what he saw, and another said she had "genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," a court previously heard.

Police bodyworn footage of Sterling's arrest at 9.15 a.m. shows him in the crashed car with two canisters on his lap as the officer tells him: "You can put that down mate."

Sterling pleaded guilty in September to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road in Surrey.

He also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation, a class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.

During the September hearing at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 7.45 a.m. and 8.52 a.m. about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven.

Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 at 7.49 a.m. after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Mr Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings -- driving on the southbound M3 at around 8.45 a.m. -- said she saw a black Lamborghini and described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes," the court heard.

"She had genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," Mr Jones told the court.

"She looked across, initially thought an air bag was in play, then realised in fact it was a large white inflated balloon and the neck of balloon was in mouth of the driver."

Dashcam footage released by the Crown Prosecution Service shows a black Lamborghini switching lanes multiple times before hitting a concrete barrier on the right side and continuing on the road.

Sterling had come off at junction 4a of the M3 before doing a loop on the A327 and, just after a roundabout, he came off the road.

The vehicle veered off the carriageway and "must have collided with either the sign or metal gate", which caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers and disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide," Mr Jones said.

He complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision, Mr Jones added.

In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer."

Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that this was a "top category case" because of prolonged driving and "at times" serious impairment which would have been short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

Sterling scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate's side reach the 2018 World Cup semifinals and the final of Euro 2020.

He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.

Sterling, who was born in Kingston, Jamaica, moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the FA Cup in 2019.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but after falling out of favour spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal.

After leaving Stamford Bridge, Sterling joined Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of the season.

He is currently without a club.

Sterling was made an MBE in the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out against racism on and off the pitch for several years.

It came amid controversy over England fans booing players taking the knee at matches as a gesture against intolerance.

stories.headline: Max Verstappen admits to 40-hour GTA VI spree as he won Las Vegas GP
stories.summary: Max Verstappen claims he had already clocked 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto VI before his brilliant Las Vegas Grand Prix win at the weekend.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen claims he had already clocked 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto VI before his brilliant Las Vegas Grand Prix win at the weekend.

Verstappen delivered a masterclass of how to race with F1's new engines to win in Sin City, a race which saw an incredible 35 lead changes, but has since revealed that much of his downtime was spent binging through Rockstar's highly-anticipated new game, which came out on Nov. 19.

Revealing the total gameplay time to teammates on the Twitch channel of his esports team, Verstappen Sim Racing, formerly known as Team Redline, he was then asked if his flight home felt like the quickest ever because of the game.

"No, I was sleeping on the plane," he replied. "I played a lot in the evening and the morning in Vegas."

The release of the game coincided with the start of the on-track schedule in Vegas.

Verstappen was one of the drivers who admitted during media day on Wednesday that he had already pre-downloaded the game ready to play, which came out at midnight leading into Thursday.

The schedule followed with two practice sessions on Nov. 19, then qualifying and the race at 8 p.m. local time on Nov. 20 and 21 respectively.

When one of his fellow Twitch streamers quipped it was time well spent, he added: "Yeah! It's not like I can go out anyway."

Verstappen later revealed he does not watch any of the cut scenes around the game's story.

"I'm over 80% of the missions," he added.

- Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc 'unmanageable' - Ferrari boss

- Lewis Hamilton: I could have beaten Kimi Antonelli if I was Ferrari No. 1

- Haas confirm Rafa Camara will finish 2026 season with the team

The admission will add another layer to what will likely go down as one of the best and most memorable grand prix performances of his storied career, which also included a brutal putdown of Mercedes rival George Russell, who he claimed is "so far below my level" that he was unfazed by criticism the British driver had made earlier in the week.

Verstappen is known for gaming at all hours during F1 weekends.

In 2024, Red Bull's then-racing advisor Helmut Marko had to ask the Dutchman to stop streaming himself playing late-night sim racing sessions with Team Redline in the middle of the night and early hours of the morning during F1 weekends.

Verstappen later said the yo-yo Vegas race was something he had only ever experienced playing Mario Kart before.

stories.headline: Sparks forward Cameron Brink, Ben Felter wed at Stanford
stories.summary: The couple met in 2021 and was engaged in 2024 before marrying at their alma mater's Memorial Church.
stories.body:
Cameron Brink and Ben Felter have officially tied the knot after holding a ceremony on Nov. 14 at their alma mater Stanford's Memorial Church.

According to a report Tuesday from Vogue Magazine, which shared behind-the-scenes details and images, the Los Angeles Sparks forward had four bridal looks, including a custom dress from bridal designer Danielle Frankel for the ceremony, and another for the reception.

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry and his wife, Ayesha, were among those in attendance. Curry and Brink are godsiblings as their fathers were teammates at Virginia Tech, and their mothers were roommates on campus.

The reception was at Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, while vows were exchanged at Memorial Church, one of the earliest interdenominational churches in the West. The waiting list to get married there can be up to four years, but alumni receive a shorter period, according to Vogue. The couple told the magazine that they always knew they wanted to wed there.

"Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day," Brink said.

Brink and Felter met at Stanford in the fall of 2020. The two began dating in March 2021 after Felter sent Brink an email in which he included his phone number. Felter, who rowed at Stanford, proposed to Brink in Paris in September 2024.

The No. 2 pick in the 2024 WNBA draft, Brink averaged a career-high 9.5 points plus five rebounds and 1.8 blocks for Los Angeles in the 2026 season.

stories.headline: Navajo Stirling belts another former champ, moves up in rankings

stories.body:
If you've ever worn a UFC light heavyweight championship belt, watch out for Navajo Stirling.

His two most recent victories have come against former 205-pound champions, both knockouts. After a first-round finish of Jan Blachowicz in August, the New Zealander knocked out Jiří Procházka in Saturday's UFC Fight Night main event in Qatar.

As a result, Stirling leapfrogs Procházka in the ESPN divisional rankings, rising to No. 3 at light heavyweight. After his fourth straight knockout overall, Stirling (12-0) is right behind the division's champion, Carlos Ulberg, Stirling's training partner at City Kickboxing in Auckland. Aljamain Sterling lost a 145-pound fight to Kevin Vallejos and drops four spots to No. 7, right below Vallejos. stories.headline: Price tag for Tassie's new AFL stadium goes up, again
stories.summary: The estimated cost of a new 23,000-seat waterfront venue, set to eventually become the home of the Tasmania Devils, has risen again.
stories.body:
Tasmania's new AFL stadium has suffered another cost blowout, causing the premier to break a promise to cap the state's spend as critics fear the end price will be far higher.

The cost estimate for the 23,000-seat roofed venue at Macquarie Point in Hobart has increased from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion.

On top of the figure is $132 million for broader precinct infrastructure, project delivery costs of $183 million and unspecified contingencies, taking the total to $1.54 billion.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff previously pledged to cap Tasmania's contribution to the build at $875 million as part of a deal to get the project through parliament.

But he conceded on Tuesday the state would have to cover the slated $100 million increase via extra borrowings.

"The previous cost estimate, which we announced ... some 14 months ago, there's been a lot of water under the bridge since that point," Mr Rockliff said.

The premier confirmed the project wouldn't head back to parliament for the approval of the necessary extra funding, despite previous assurances it would.

The latest estimate reflects increases in the cost of construction, sustained high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and its complexity, the state government said.

The stadium is expected to be ready for the 2031 AFL season and was a condition of the Tasmania Devils being granted a licence to enter into the national competition in 2028.

It initially had a price tag of $715 million.

Mr Rockliff said the state had reached out to the federal government and AFL for extra money on top of their $240 million and $15 million contributions.

Anti-stadium group Our Place Hobart said the new cost estimate failed to take into account other factors, including the interest bill and the exact cost of contingencies.

Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff described the ongoing cost increases as a deep betrayal of Tasmanians.

"Who knows where the final price for the stadium will end up?" she said.

"What we do know is there's been now a fifth major cost blowout and there's not yet a contract price locked in for this massive project."

Federal independent MP Andrew Wilkie fears the stadium will end up costing $2 billion.

"Once you add the cost of the debt over a decade, the total cost to the Tasmanian taxpayer is closer to $3.5 billion," he said.

Devils chief executive Brendon Gale said the question of any additional funding from the AFL was a matter for the sport's governing body.

"The politicians can politic. We'll get on with building our club," he said.

"People have their views and are entitled to them. But based on my experience, people never look back. These types of projects transform cities and states."

The release of updated costs came ahead of schedule after the government bowed to political pressure to make the figures public before the end of the parliamentary year.

In mid-October, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder. A final contract is set to be signed by the end of 2026.

BESIX Watpac recently built a 30,000-seat roofed stadium in Christchurch in New Zealand which cost about $540 million.

Mr Rockliff said the final contract price for the Hobart stadium was unlikely to differ from the $1.23 billion estimate.

The stadium has been deeply divisive in Tasmania amid rising state debt, a stretched health system and other under-pressure services.

The AFL and federal government have been contacted for comment.

stories.headline: 'Can't judge them': who Papenhuyzen wants at the Storm
stories.summary: Ex-Melbourne star Ryan Papenhuyzen has made some big calls on who should be the next Storm coach and the one to keep from Cameron Munster and Harry Grant.
stories.body:
Ryan Papenhuyzen empathises with Cameron Munster but believes Melbourne must prioritise keeping Harry Grant if the NRL powerhouse can't hold on to both superstars.

Munster on Tuesday rejected an offer from the Storm believed to be for one year with the option of another season, labelling the terms "disappointing".

The Storm are also fighting to keep Grant, and Papenhuyzen was unequivocal when asked on Wednesday who the club should target if salary-cap pressures meant only one of the newly crowned Australian World Cup winners could stay.

"I went through something similar as Munster where I thought the club had low-balled me," the happily retired 2020 premiership-winning hero told AAP.

"But having my time out of the game now, they've got their reasons for offering those certain amounts and it might not be enough (for Munster).

"Penrith have done it for years and years. They get to a point where they can't hold their players and they've got a price for their players.

"So I understand Munster's perspective. He wants to earn as much as he can in his career and he wants to win a premiership, so that probably limits his opportunities.

"If a club's got money and they're in a premiership window, it's probably a good chance he'll go to that club."

At 28, skipper Grant is four years younger than Munster and more important long-term to the Storm, Papenhuyzen believes.

"Harry's done a brilliant job in terms of leadership," the ex-Clive Churchill Medallist turned caddy said after playing in the Australian PGA Championship pro-am in Sydney.

"The amount of care he has for everyone in that group and the way he thinks about the game, I feel really sorry for him over the last 12 months (when Melbourne missed the finals) because he's always trying to find new ideas to bring everyone.

"He's a great leader for that club going forward. I'd hate to see him go because he's a player you want to build a club around and I guess Munster is towards the back end of his career.

"He had a great World Cup, but World Cups are different to NRL seasons. You've got to lock in for a month with that, and an NRL season's a long time."

Pressed on who he'd keep as a priority, Papenhuyzen said: "Harry's probably the one leadership-wise. Just his qualities are really admirable.

"You know what Munster brings to the game. He gives you confidence standing next to him, knowing what he's going do, but I just think Harry ..."

With coach Craig Bellamy confirming he is moving on at the end of 2027, Papenhuyzen also suspects Grant might be a better for the Storm's new mentor, whomever that may be.

"Harry's really respected and in terms of trying to keep the culture, he's very open-minded too," the BMW golf correspondent said.

"He's open to new ideas, whereas Munster is very much like Bellamy - he's sort of got his way and it's worked for him for so long.

"Whatever they both decide to do, you can't judge them. It's never a right or wrong decision."

Papenhuyzen believes it would be "awesome" if Billy Slater succeeded Bellamy, but suspects "life is too good" for the Storm legend to be a head NRL coach.

"I love Jyles. If he went back there, I'd be awfully encouraged of how well they're going to go. They'd probably be my two."

But Papenhuyzen, also open to helping out the new coach, nominated Bellamy's son Aaron as a left-field option.

"Aaron's awesome with people," he said.

"He's awesome with the wider playing group and he understands that Craig sometimes pushes the boundaries. Aaron's a bit more like Wendy - Craig's, Craig's wife.

"They're both a bit more more gentle, so you've got that loving, nurturing side and potentially (he could do the job).

"I do know you just need people around you. We'd be silly to say the coach controls everything."

stories.headline: Inside LeBron's first game in Philly -- more than two decades ago
stories.summary: Nearly 25 years ago, LeBron won over Philly for the first time -- inside one of the most iconic basketball arenas in the world.
stories.body:
THE FAX LAID out a grandiose plan.

Jeremy Treatman, a former high school assistant coach in the Philadelphia suburbs who was running a burgeoning company that staged big-time basketball events between the game's future stars, had just sent a message to Dru Joyce II, the new coach at St. Vincent-St. Mary High School in Akron, Ohio, the school famously led by one of the most highly touted prep prospects in the history of the sport.

It was the summer of 2002.

Six months after a then-17-year-old LeBron James had appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated accompanied by the headline, "The Chosen One," Treatman was pitching Joyce on choosing him to build James' hype even more.

How would you like to play at the Palestra in Philly? How would you like to play Madison Square Garden against Sebastian Telfair? How would you like to play at Ohio State? How would you like to play at University of Dayton? How would you like to play in the Dean Dome in North Carolina?

In Philly parlance, Treatman had him at, "Yo."

"He calls me the next day and he says, 'You can get us to play at the Palestra?!'" Treatman told ESPN. "I go, 'Absolutely! Of course.' He goes, 'I've always dreamed of playing in the Palestra. I've heard about this place my whole life.

"We're in.'"

There was only one problem.

"I was completely bluffing about the Palestra," Treatman said. "I hadn't talked to anybody."

NAMED BY UNIVERSITY of Pennsylvania professor William N. Bates, evoking the Greek term "palæstra" that describes an athletic competition surrounded by an audience, the Palestra was the home for Penn's basketball, volleyball and wrestling teams.

But its reputation as a hoops haven spread far beyond the corner of S. 33rd St. and Walnut St. on the Quakers' campus.

With its red brick facade, its ceiling suspended by a spine of steel arches and bleachers that practically bleed right onto the maple hardwood playing surface, the Palestra became more than just a gymnasium, earning the nickname "The Cathedral of College Basketball."

It was for decades the home for the famed round-robin Big Five schedule between Philadelphia's college basketball teams and has hosted more NCAA men's basketball games than any other arena in the country.

"Brad Stevens and I, when I worked for him in Boston, we would go back and forth about Hinkle or the Palestra, Hinkle or the Palestra," Detroit Pistons assistant coach Jerome Allen told ESPN.

Allen, a Penn alum, took umbrage with his old boss' preference for Butler University's bandbox.

"[The Palestra] was built in 1926," Allen continued. "The first college game was played in '27. Cameron Indoor Stadium [at Duke University] was modeled after it. And everybody played in it: high school, college. It's a who's who for college basketball."

(The NBA might have sided with Stevens by opting to have the NBA Cup final at Hinkle Fieldhouse this December. But Evan Wasch, the NBA's executive vice president of basketball strategy and growth, recently said the Palestra is "on the list" for consideration to host a future cup championship.)

It was the perfect stage, Treatman thought, to host James, whom he first saw play in person at the Slam Dunk to the Beach tournament in Lewes, Delaware, in December 2001.

"I saw him make an under-the-basket reverse layup that reminded me of Dr. J's move over Mark Landsberger," Treatman said, referring to Julius Erving's iconic bucket for the Philadelphia 76ers in Game 4 of the 1980 NBA Finals against the Los Angeles Lakers.

Treatman pulled out his cellphone.

With the image of a soaring James still fresh in his mind, he dialed Gregg Downer, the head coach at Lower Merion High School, where Treatman used to work as an assistant.

"I called Downer and I said, 'I can't believe what I'm saying, but I think I just saw somebody who might be better than Kobe [Bryant],'" Treatman recalled.

While Joyce prepared his team for James' senior season, Treatman began to make good on his bluff.

He called Peggy Kowalski, the Palestra's box office manager, to get her on board, telling her he was "almost positive" the event would sell out.

Now he just needed an opponent. He wanted to keep it local.

"My idea was not to have them play the best team [in the country], but the best Philly team," Treatman said.

He settled on Strawberry Mansion, a Philadelphia Public League school whose star, 6-foot-2 guard Maureece Rice, was threatening to break the high school scoring record of the man responsible for the most famous 100-point game in history: Wilt Chamberlain.

The game was set: St. Vincent-St. Mary vs. Strawberry Mansion. James vs. Rice. Dec. 22, 2002, at the Palestra.

"To have Bron there," Allen said, "everybody talked about the battle between him and Reece Rice."

FIVE YEARS BEFORE Aron Cohen scored 14 points off the bench to help lift Penn over the Princeton Tigers as a junior guard, he was a high school sophomore sitting in the stands, soaking in the most raucous basketball environment he ever experienced -- before or since.

"I just remember the Palestra being so packed," Cohen told ESPN. "I mean, when I played at Penn, we played against Carolina when they were No. 1 in the country.

"And from what I remember, I felt like that game against LeBron was more packed. ... Just hearing about him, seeing him in SLAM magazine, it was like, 'Wow, this guy is in another world.' You have to see him. You can't miss it if you're a basketball fan."

Former Detroit Pistons guard Richard Hamilton, whose Coatesville, Pennsylvania, high school team lost to Bryant and Lower Merion in the district playoffs at the Palestra in 1996, distinctly remembers the landmark game.

"The Palestra is a big deal for us. That was always the mecca of Philadelphia for us," Hamilton told ESPN. "So when LeBron James comes there ... that was a moment for Philadelphia. Because it was before social media. Nobody got an opportunity to see him. So when you see this man-child coming to the arena with the type of aura that came with it, it was something that my friends and my family talk about to this day."

Treatman delivered on his sellout prognostication -- and then some.

"I had random people coming up to my office on the sixth floor at 1420 Walnut St., knocking on the door: 'You selling tickets? You selling tickets?'" Treatman said. "And I was. I was selling tickets. It was a one-man ticket office. It was hysterical. The phone calls were just nonstop. And the game, they tell me there were more people in the Palestra that night than any time in history."

Among the attendees were current New York Knicks president of basketball operations Leon Rose, a then-influential sports agent who eventually signed James as a client. William Wesley, one of the sport's biggest power brokers, made an appearance. Cantankerous (and ubiquitous) Philadelphia sports radio personality Howard Eskin was there. A handful of Eagles players.

Sixers star Allen Iverson -- just a year removed from winning MVP and taking Philadelphia all the way to the Finals against Bryant, Shaquille O'Neal and the Lakers -- was in the stands.

But for James' team -- that had lost high-profile games the season before against other prominent foes in Oak Hill Academy (Virigina) and Amityville (New York) -- it was still a business trip.

"I always speak about the abnormal becoming normal for us," said Romeo Travis, one of James' high school teammates who went on to become the University of Akron's all-time blocked shots leader before a long pro career overseas.

"So we knew Iverson was coming, but it wasn't like, 'Oh my god, we got to play good for Iverson.' It was just like, 'OK.' It wasn't disrespectful or anything, because Iverson was still the man at that time, but it was just like, Shaq had just come to see us play."

James' team was 6-0 to start the season, including a revenge 20-point victory over Oak Hill 10 days before, and was ranked No. 9 in the country, according to USA Today.

They smashed Strawberry Mansion.

SVSM went up 36-15 in the first half, using a full-court press that the home team couldn't handle.

"The game was pretty much over pretty quickly," Cohen said. "St. Mary's was just way better. And LeBron had [an] early dunk and just set the whole place off, like, 'Ooh.'"

Rice came into the game needing 80 points to break Chamberlain's Philadelphia high school scoring record of 2,252 points.

He had zero at the break on 0-for-6 shooting.

"The fans were on the floor talking crazy like, 'Yo, y'all stink! [Coming from] these cornfields [in Ohio]' and all that stuff," Travis remembered. "It was really cool, though. That was my favorite part about the experience, was the fans."

Treatman, who now admits he "let in at least 150 extra people" beyond the 8,700-person Palestra capacity, started to get antsy.

This wasn't what the proud Philly crowd came -- and paid -- to see.

"It got really raunchy," Treatman said. "Gloria James got up and riled up the crowd. I thought there was going to be a riot. It was getting a little ugly in there."

That's when LeBron James, nearly 25 years before signing with the Sixers and sending the city into another frenzy as a 41-year-old, won over Philly for the first time.

THE SCORE HAD swelled to 65-25 in his team's favor after three quarters when James adjusted the game plan -- for both teams.

When Rice hit a 3 early in the fourth quarter for just his second made basket of the night, James called for a clearout on Rice and pulled up to answer with a 3 of his own.

Rice brought the ball up the floor and James stayed on him. Then Rice called for a clearout, too, feeling the juice of their back-and-forth.

When Rice reached the wing, just above the 3-point line, he crossed his dribble left to right. James took a step backward, anticipating a drive, and both sneakers slipped underneath him.

Rice crossed back through his legs, right to left, and with James scrambling to get back up from the floor, fired up another 3.

He airballed the shot, but the mano-a-mano matchup was exactly what the fans had paid to see.

Possession by possession, the Palestra's walls pulsated with their every move.

"I've never heard a place louder than that ... ever," Cohen said.

James came back down the court and answered with another 3.

"This is when I realized LeBron James was a brilliant young man ... he noticed what was going on," Treatman said. "He felt the buzz, he felt the tension, and he called Maureece Rice over during live game action. He waved eight people away and they played one-on-one for four minutes.

"They went up and down. Nobody else touched the ball for four minutes, and it was the most brilliant, incredible thing I've ever seen."

Where Treatman saw showmanship, Travis saw a competitive zeal, the kind that has sustained his childhood friend through an NBA career in its 24th season.

"How he became who he became is he didn't duck anybody," Travis said. "Anybody that said they were somebody, you had to show him proof. And Maureece Rice, even though they played different positions, they were saying he was one of the best in the country. OK, you're going to have to show and prove that. And you're going to have to come, and even if the game's over, you're going to have to show me something."

James finished with 26 points, seven rebounds and seven assists.

Rice, thanks to the late surge, ended up scoring 13. St. Vincent-St. Mary went on to win 85-47.

"Growing up and being a historian and reading stories about the Palestra ... for us to go there my senior year, being from Akron, I was like, 'Oh, man, I'm in the building with some of the greatest that's ever played," James recalled on a recent episode of his podcast, "Mind the Game," with co-host Steve Nash.

"It just had an aura about it, when I played there. It was fun."

Nash asked James what stood out from his memories about the game all these years later: Iverson in the crowd and the name of his fourth-quarter rival in that packed gym in Philly, James said.

"We were playing the No. 1 player in Pennsylvania, Maureece Rice," James added. "I'm reading all this stuff about Wilt and the history of the game, and we're traveling to Philadelphia. ... It was like, 'Oh shoot, we better have our shoes [tied] tight and we better be ready to go.'"

Rice is 42 now, about six months older than James. He rarely posts anything about his basketball career on his Instagram account. But scroll down to 2021 and the second slide of a post showing an adolescent Rice cheesing for the camera while wearing a white No. 14 Charles Barkley USA Basketball jersey is a grainy clip of James talking about their showdown.

"I respect Maureece a lot. He's one of the great players I've ever played against. I'm confident in him and I hope he keeps working. If he keeps working, he'll be a great player."

Rice went on to play four years for George Washington University and spent a week on the Sixers' training camp roster in 2008 before continuing his career in the G League and abroad.

James, in his first season in Philadelphia, has helped lead the Sixers to an 8-1 start, hoping to add to the four championships on his résumé before retiring.

Cohen, who's fighting cancer, still plays pickup games at Penn on Saturday mornings. Watching James play basketball in Philadelphia gives him an escape just like it did when he was a high school kid.

"I'm still in shock," Cohen said. "I'm like, 'LeBron James is a Sixer.' It's still surreal to me. ... I mean, for me personally, it's literally one of the most exciting, cool things to do in my life right now, is to just watch him and be a part of just the hoopla of knowing he's on our team."

Travis spent time this summer golfing and hanging out with James and some of their high school teammates. He'll go see James and the Sixers play in person when Philadelphia rolls through Cleveland and Detroit this season -- easy car rides from his Ohio home.

He would have seen him a lot more often had James signed with the Cavaliers, but he doesn't hold it against him.

"I was confused, but I understood. He wanted to win," Travis said. "And I understand that, that he just wants to win and whatever it takes. I understand that completely and respect it. ... One of the great things about him is he does it his way."

Treatman organized another showcase event featuring St. Vincent-St. Mary 17 years later in Columbus, Ohio, with James' alma mater facing Sierra Canyon High School, where James' son Bronny played.

James squeezed in a visit to watch his son play in the game during a Lakers off day.

It provided some full-circle nostalgia for Treatman, but even he says it wasn't the same as that December day in Philadelphia more than two decades ago.

"It was something you've never seen before," he said. " [And] you've never seen again."
